title: Given a Scenario, Troubleshoot Deployment Issues

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud deployments can fail even when the design looks correct on paper.
Troubleshooting deployment issues means identifying what prevents a workload from being created, starting, scaling, or operating correctly.
CompTIA focuses on incompatibility, misconfigurations, outdated definitions, deprecated functionality, outages, resource limits, and regional availability.
The main mental model is: What changed, what is missing, and what limit or incompatibility is blocking deployment?

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Is the deployment failing because the resource cannot run, is configured incorrectly, is unsupported, has hit a limit, or is unavailable where it is being deployed?
sections.callout: Deployment failure → check compatibility, configuration, support status, resource limits, and regional service availability.

sections.title: Incompatibility
paragraphs: An incompatibility occurs when two components, platforms, versions, or resource requirements cannot work together correctly.
Examples include an application requiring an unavailable feature, an image being incompatible with the chosen architecture, or one software version not supporting another component.
Think: These pieces do not fit together.
sections.callout: Technologies or versions cannot work together → incompatibility.

sections.title: Misconfigurations
paragraphs: A deployment may contain all the correct components but still fail because they were configured incorrectly.

entries.title: Resource Allocation
paragraphs: Resource allocation determines how much compute, memory, storage, or other capacity is assigned. Too little can prevent a workload from functioning.
Think: The workload did not receive what it needs.
entries.recognitionCue: The deployment lacks enough assigned resources → resource allocation misconfiguration.

entries.title: Permission Issues
paragraphs: A deployment process may need permission to create resources, attach storage, access images, configure networks, and use APIs.
If those rights are missing, deployment can fail even when the template is correct.
Think: The deployment knows what to do, but it is not allowed to do it.
entries.recognitionCue: An operation fails with access denied or insufficient privileges → permission issue.

entries.title: Oversubscription
paragraphs: Oversubscription occurs when more resources are promised or allocated than the underlying infrastructure can realistically provide at the same time.
It can lead to poor performance, resource contention, and deployment failures.
Think: More seats were sold than the plane has.
entries.recognitionCue: Too many workloads are competing for limited underlying resources → oversubscription.

entries.title: Sizing Issues
paragraphs: A sizing issue occurs when the selected resource size is too small, too large, or the wrong type for the workload.
Think: Wrong-size box.
entries.recognitionCue: The instance shape or resource size does not meet workload needs → sizing issue.

sections.title: Outdated Component Definitions
paragraphs: Cloud deployment templates and definitions may reference versions, images, packages, or components that are no longer current.
An outdated definition can fail when the referenced item no longer exists, is unsupported, has changed, or requires newer syntax.
Think: The deployment instructions are asking for yesterday's component.
sections.callout: A template references an old image, package, or resource definition → outdated component definition.

sections.title: Deprecation of Functionality
paragraphs: Deprecation means functionality is being retired or is no longer recommended and may eventually stop working.
A deployment relying on deprecated functionality can fail after the provider removes or disables it.
Think: It used to work, but the platform has moved on.
sections.callout: A previously supported feature has been phased out → deprecation of functionality.

sections.title: Outages
paragraphs: Cloud services can experience outages. CompTIA distinguishes full and partial impact.

entries.title: Full Outage
paragraphs: A full outage means the service is completely unavailable. Think: Nothing works.
entries.recognitionCue: All users or all service functionality is unavailable → full outage.

entries.title: Partial Outage
paragraphs: A partial outage affects only part of the service, such as one region, one feature, some users, or some resources.
Think: Something works, something does not.
entries.recognitionCue: Only part of the environment is affected → partial outage.

sections.title: Resource Limits
paragraphs: Cloud providers place limits on how many requests or resources a customer can consume.

entries.title: API Throttling
paragraphs: API throttling limits how many API requests can be made within a given period.
If automation sends too many requests too quickly, the provider may reject or delay requests.
Think: Slow down—you are calling the API too fast.
entries.recognitionCue: Deployment automation fails after sending too many API requests → API throttling.

entries.title: Service Quotas
paragraphs: A service quota limits how many resources or how much capacity an account can use, such as instances, addresses, storage, or networks.
Think: You reached your allowed maximum.
entries.recognitionCue: The account cannot create another resource because a provider limit was reached → service quota.

table.caption: Resource-limit comparison
rows: Too many resources or too much capacity

sections.title: Regional Service Availability
paragraphs: Not every cloud service or resource type exists in every region.
A deployment may fail because the selected region does not provide the requested service.
Think: The cloud provider has it—but not there.
sections.callout: A resource exists at the provider but not in the selected region → regional service availability.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Technologies cannot work together → Incompatibility
Too few resources are assigned → Resource allocation
Access is denied during deployment → Permission issue
Too many workloads share limited infrastructure → Oversubscription
The instance is too small, too large, or the wrong shape → Sizing issue
A template references an old component → Outdated component definition
A feature has been phased out → Deprecation
The entire service is unavailable → Full outage
Only part of the service is unavailable → Partial outage
Too many API calls occur → API throttling
The maximum number of resources is reached → Service quota
The service is unavailable in the selected region → Regional service availability

entries.title: Oversubscription vs. Sizing
paragraphs: Oversubscription means too many workloads are competing for shared capacity. Sizing means one workload has the wrong resource size.

entries.title: API Throttling vs. Service Quota
paragraphs: Both can block automation. Requests per period indicate API throttling; allowed resource quantity indicates a service quota.

entries.title: Outdated vs. Deprecated
paragraphs: Outdated means an old definition or version. Deprecated means functionality is intentionally being phased out.

entries.title: Full vs. Partial Outage
paragraphs: Full means the service is gone. Partial means only some users, features, or resources are affected.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Components cannot work together → Incompatibility
Not enough assigned CPU, RAM, or storage → Resource allocation

Too many workloads compete for host capacity → Oversubscription
Wrong instance size → Sizing issue
Template references an old image or version → Outdated component definition
Feature is being retired → Deprecation
Everything is unavailable → Full outage
Only some functionality is unavailable → Partial outage
Too many API requests → API throttling
Maximum allowed resources reached → Service quota
